name: ARTEX and the South Korean bank breaches (2026)
blurb: Between late September and early October 2026 attackers broke into South Korean financial institutions and took customer data out. CrowdStrike's report of 7 October says an unattributed threat actor, likely Chinese-speaking and financially motivated, did it with ARTEX, an open-source AI penetration testing tool, running on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, plus Claude Code sessions on Zhipu AI's GLM-5.3 and xAI's Grok 4.6. The evidence came from the attacker's own servers, whose open directories exposed Claude Code session histories and a Chinese-language pentesting prompt. The way in was the systems around the banks, a broker-facing loan inquiry service and an employee mobile app, not their core ledgers. Korean investigators have not established ARTEX's role, and the account of AI agents doing the work comes from CrowdStrike.
teaser: An open-source AI pentest tool, four providers' models and an attacker's exposed sessions: how South Korean banks were breached in 2026, and six lessons for defenders.
subtitle: A case study in AI-run intrusion: the open-source agent, the four models, the exposed sessions, and what defenders should take from it
body_html:
What happened

The campaign ran from late September to early October 2026 against South Korean financial organizations, and data was exfiltrated. Korean authorities, as reported in the Korean press, say at least seven financial firms were affected and the personal data of about 68,000 people was taken; CrowdStrike says the number of affected organizations is unconfirmed. The entry points were not core banking systems: at one bank, a loan progress inquiry service used by financial brokers; at another, a mobile work support system for employees. Korean regulators have said payment credentials that would allow unauthorized transactions were not taken, according to the same press reports. CrowdStrike does not attribute the campaign to a named adversary and assesses, with moderate confidence, that the actor is Chinese-speaking and financially motivated.

The AI stack

ComponentWhat CrowdStrike says it did
ARTEXOpen-source AI penetration testing tool, Chinese-developed, released on GitHub on 26 July 2026. Ran the intrusion work.
DeepSeek v4.1 FlashARTEX's primary language model backend, probably reached through an LLM API reseller.
Claude CodeAgentic coding sessions whose histories and memory files, including a CLAUDE.md with a Chinese-language pentesting prompt, sat in open directories on the attacker's servers.
GLM-5.3 (Zhipu AI) and Grok 4.6 (xAI)Models used for additional Claude Code sessions.
InfrastructureTwo servers: a Hong Kong IP as primary infrastructure and a second host running ARTEX, with nine proxy IPs.

The sessions also show the actor asking Claude where Korean breach data is sold and for help finding Korean Telegram groups that trade it. CrowdStrike's reading is that the tooling let one financially motivated actor run several intrusions in a short span.

How it was found

  • 2 October 2026. The Kyunghyang Shinmun reported that the Genians Security Center found the string ARTEX in the HTML titles of attack servers used against Shinhan Bank and other institutions.
  • 4 October. Kyunghyang reported ARTEX's 26 July GitHub release; the head of the Financial Security Institute said the attackers could not be identified from IP addresses alone.
  • 6 October. Yonhap reported that AhnLab found ARTEX instances on about 600 IP addresses, a measure of where the tool is hosted, not of who used it.
  • 7 October. CrowdStrike Intelligence published its report, built on the attacker's exposed directories.

What is established, and what is not

Established by CrowdStrike: the AI tooling, the models, the two-server infrastructure, the exposed session histories and prompts, the entry points, and the MITRE techniques below. Reported by Korean authorities through the press: the count of affected firms and people. Not established: ARTEX's role in each breach, which Korean investigators have not confirmed; who the actor is; and how many organizations were affected in total. The report also lists personal details typed into a prompt that CrowdStrike says it cannot definitively associate with the actor. This site does not publish them, on this page, in its news coverage or in its data.

Six lessons for defenders

  1. Agents drop the cost of each attempt to almost nothing. One actor ran several intrusions in a short span because the tooling did the repetitive work.
  2. The perimeter is the brokers, contractors and employee apps. Both named entry points were systems built for people outside the core, which is where third-party and supply chain risk lives.
  3. Spending is not security. Korean press reports put the data protection spending of Shinhan, KB Kookmin and Hana at about 124 billion won last year.
  4. Open-source agents are dual use. ARTEX was released in July and remains public; a penetration testing tool is also an attack tool.
  5. One model's safeguards do not stop a multi-model operator. The actor moved between four providers' models and asked a commercial model for help selling stolen data. See AI agent security.
  6. Attribution is weak, but fingerprints and opsec failures still catch attackers. A string in an HTML title and an open directory exposed the operation.

Companies named

Anthropic (Claude Code), DeepSeek (DeepSeek v4.1 Flash), Zhipu AI (GLM-5.3) and xAI (Grok 4.6). Naming a model here records what the attacker used; it is not a finding against the provider. Related topics: AI-enabled malware and AI red teaming.
